1. The Literal Meaning

"Et al." is a short Latin expression. It is an abbreviation for "et alii" (or its variations et aliae or et alia, depending on grammar), which simply means "and others."

That's the heart of it. When you see "et al.," your brain should immediately read: "and others."

Latin was the universal language of scholars, scientists, and legal professionals in Europe for centuries. Many abbreviations and phrases from that era are still used today in academic and professional writing because they became deeply embedded in global scholarly tradition. "Et al." is one of the most common survivors of that tradition.

Breaking it down word by word:

  • "Et" = "and" (you can also see this in the ampersand symbol &, which evolved from a stylized et)
  • "Al." = an abbreviation of alii (others)

So: et + al. = and + others = "and others."
3. Why It Exists — The Problem It Solves

Imagine a scientific research paper written by eight different authors. Every time you cite that paper in your own writing, do you really have to write all eight names? That would be long, repetitive, and cluttered.

"Et al." solves this problem elegantly. Instead of writing:

Johnson, M., Smith, R., Patel, A., Williams, D., Chen, L., Kumar, S., Okafor, B., & Rossi, F. (2023)

You can write:

Johnson et al. (2023)

Clean. Simple. Precise. Everyone knows it means Johnson and the other authors of that work.

"Et al." appears in three main areas:

A. Academic and Scientific Writing (Most Common Use)

When citing a source — a book, article, or study — that has multiple authors, writers use "et al." to avoid listing every name repeatedly. It is standard in research papers, dissertations, journals, and textbooks.

B. Legal Documents

In law, a case or lawsuit can involve many parties (plaintiffs or defendants). Legal documents use "et al." to indicate there are more parties than the one named. For example:

Smith et al. v. National Bank

This means Smith and other people (perhaps other co-plaintiffs) are suing the National Bank together.

C. General Formal Writing

Occasionally, formal reports or official documents use "et al." when listing contributors, signatories, or members of a group where naming every individual would be impractical.

This is where many people make mistakes. Let's be precise:

Correct: et al.

Here are the specific rules:

  • "et" has no period after it. It is a complete Latin word (et = "and"), not an abbreviation, so it needs no period.
  • "al." has a period after it. It is an abbreviation (of alii/aliae/alia), so the period is mandatory.
  • The expression is written entirely in lowercase, unless it falls at the very start of a sentence (which is rare and best avoided).
  • In many formal academic contexts, "et al." is written in italics because it is a foreign (Latin) phrase. However, many modern style guides (like the latest editions of APA and MLA) no longer require italics. When in doubt, follow the style guide your field uses.

(An exception: if "et al." begins a sentence — which good writers generally avoid — only then would you capitalize the E.)
6. The Grammar Rule — When Exactly Do You Use It?

Different citation style guides (the rulebooks that different academic fields follow) have slightly different thresholds, but the general principle is the same: use "et al." when there are too many authors to list comfortably.

Here's how the major style guides handle it:

APA Style (7th Edition) — used widely in psychology, social sciences, and education:

  • If a work has 3 or more authors, use "et al." from the very first time you cite it.
  • Example: (Williams et al., 2021)

MLA Style (9th Edition) — used widely in humanities and literature:

  • If a work has 3 or more authors, list only the first author's name followed by "et al."
  • Example: (Williams et al. 45) — where 45 is the page number.

Chicago Style — used in history, arts, and some social sciences:

  • For works with 4 or more authors, you may use "et al." after the first author's name.

The specific threshold varies, but the spirit is consistent: "et al." kicks in when listing every name becomes impractical.
7. "Et al." Is NOT the Same as These Other Latin Abbreviations

Since "et al." lives alongside other Latin abbreviations, it helps to know what it is not:

  • "etc." (et cetera) = "and so on" / "and other things." You use etc. for things or items in a list, not for people. You would never write "Johnson, Smith, etc." in a citation — that's what et al. is for.
  • "e.g." (exempli gratia) = "for example."
  • "i.e." (id est) = "that is" / "in other words."
  • "cf." (confer) = "compare."

The key distinction: "et al." is specifically for people, while "etc." is for things.
8. A Practical Example in Full Context

Suppose a 2022 study on climate change was authored by six scientists: Carter, Nguyen, Osei, Braun, Tanaka, and Petrov.

In your research paper, the first time you cite them:

Carter et al. (2022) found that global temperatures rose significantly over the past decade.

In the reference list at the end of your paper, however, most style guides require you to list all authors in full — "et al." is used in the body text of your writing, not in the bibliography/reference list (though some styles allow it there for very large author groups).

"Et al." is typically read aloud as:

  • "et al" (rhymes with "let pal") — short and clipped, or
  • Sometimes fully said as "et alii" in formal speech, though this is rare.

In everyday academic conversation, people simply say "and others" or "and colleagues."
Summary — The Core Idea in One Paragraph

"Et al." is a Latin abbreviation meaning "and others." It is used in academic, scientific, and legal writing as a shorthand when a source has multiple authors or parties, allowing writers to name just the first and skip the rest. It is always written as two words with a period only after "al." — never after "et." Different citation styles (APA, MLA, Chicago) have slightly different rules about exactly how many authors trigger its use, but the purpose is always the same: clarity and brevity without sacrificing accuracy.
